title: If Dark Matter Exerts a Faint 'Pressure'… Korea Astronomy and Space Science Institute Offers New Solution to the Cosmic Expansion Puzzle

content:
New research suggests that dark matter, which makes up about 27% of the universe's mass but remains unidentified, may exert an extremely faint "pressure," contrary to prevailing assumptions. The Korea Astronomy and Space Science Institute (KASI) announced on the 28th that a research team led by Drs. Shafieloo Arman and Zhang Junchen has proposed a new model that jointly analyzes the properties of dark matter and dark energy to explain recent observations of the universe's expansion. The study was published in the October 10 issue of the international journal The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

Standard cosmology holds that the universe consists of 68% dark energy, 27% dark matter, and 5% ordinary matter, with dark energy driving the universe's accelerating expansion. Dark matter neither emits nor reflects light, so it cannot be observed directly, but it influences galactic motion and the formation of cosmic structure through gravity; in the standard model it is treated as a substance with zero pressure. As the universe expands, its density is assumed to decline at the same rate as ordinary matter.

The trouble emerged from recent measurements of galaxy and quasar distances by the U.S. Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), which raised the possibility that dark energy is not an eternal constant but may be weakening over time. Explaining this within the existing theoretical framework would require assuming a complex evolution in which the ratio of dark energy's pressure to its energy density (w) crosses the "phantom boundary" at -1—a theoretically difficult territory to handle.

Rather than adjusting only the dark energy side, the researchers focused on the still-unknown properties of dark matter, judging that the long-held premise that its pressure is exactly zero may not necessarily be correct. To test this, they combined DESI's cosmic distance data, five years of supernova observations from the Dark Energy Survey (DES), and cosmic microwave background (CMB) data carrying traces of the early universe.

The results matched recent observations well when dark matter was assumed to carry a very small amount of pressure. In that case, dark matter density declines slightly faster than ordinary matter as the universe expands, and that subtle difference explains the observational data without any complex evolution of dark energy. The team produced a model consistent with the data in which dark energy does not cross the phantom boundary.

The new model can also be used to address the subtle discrepancy between estimates of the amount of dark matter in the early universe and in the present-day universe. Its agreement with observational data came out slightly higher than that of the existing model, which assumes dark energy crosses the phantom boundary.

The researchers, however, drew a line, saying the difference is not statistically significant. Current data alone cannot determine which explanation is correct. "The significance is that we have presented a new possibility for explaining recent cosmic observations without assuming complex changes in dark energy," said Arman, the lead researcher. "In particular, by departing from the long-held assumption that dark matter behaves in the same way as ordinary matter, it shows the need to take a fresh look at the physical properties of dark matter."

The methodology of this study differs in direction from experiments attempting to detect particles directly. "The IceCube experiment, which won this year's Nobel Prize in Physics, is on the front line of the search for neutrinos produced when dark matter decays or annihilates," said Kim Jinho, director of KASI's Center for Cosmic Evolution Research. "If that experiment is an attempt to catch particles directly, this study traces the properties of dark matter backward from the big picture of cosmic expansion history—and the identity of dark matter lies where the two approaches meet."

Starting next year, the team plans to continue follow-up research through K-COSMOS, a dark matter research project integrating observation, simulation, and theory. As an attempt to verify the subtle variable of dark matter pressure through precision observations, attention is focused on whether accumulating data may prompt a rewrite of the very premises of standard cosmology.
